questions.question: What does a `class` actually create in JavaScript? How do instance methods end up shared between objects?
questions.answer: A class creates a constructor function plus a `prototype` object. Methods declared in the class body are defined once on `Class.prototype`, non-enumerable. `new Class()` creates an object whose `[[Prototype]]` is `Class.prototype`, so every instance finds the same method function through the prototype chain instead of owning a copy. Class bodies are strict, are not hoisted (TDZ), and cannot be called without `new`.
key_points: A class is a constructor function under the hood.
Methods live on `Class.prototype`, not on instances.
Instances link to the prototype via `new`.
Classes are always strict and live in the TDZ.

questions.question: How do `static` members differ from instance members, and what is `this` inside a static method?
questions.answer: Instance members are reached through an object (`new User().name`) and live on the instance or its prototype. Static members live on the constructor function itself (`User.count`) and are not available on instances. Inside a static method, `this` is the class that was called — the subclass when inherited — which is why `static create() { return new this(); }` returns the right subclass. `static {}` blocks run once at class evaluation.
key_points: Statics belong to the class, not instances.
`this` in a static method is the called class/subclass.
Static members are inherited by subclasses.
`static {}` runs once during class definition.

questions.question: What do `#private` fields guarantee that an underscore convention does not? What happens when you access one on the wrong object?
questions.answer: A `#` field is enforced by the language: the name is only accessible inside the class body, it is invisible to `Object.keys`, `JSON.stringify`, and bracket access, and access is brand-checked. Reading `other.#balance` where `other` is not an instance of that class throws `TypeError`. An underscore field is just a normal public property that anyone can read or overwrite.
key_points: `#` is real encapsulation, enforced at parse/runtime.
Private names are not string keys and do not appear in enumeration.
Brand checks throw `TypeError` for foreign objects.
The field must be declared in the class body.

questions.question: Create an `Admin` class that extends `User`, adds a `level` field, calls the parent constructor, and overrides `describe()` to include the parent description.
key_points: Call `super(name)` before using `this`.
`super.describe()` calls the parent method with the same `this`.
`instanceof` passes for both the subclass and parent.
Do not duplicate parent setup manually when `super` exists.

questions.question: Add a validated `age` accessor to `User`. The setter must reject values below 0 or above 150 with a `RangeError`, and the getter must return the stored value.
key_points: Use a private backing field (`#age`) to avoid setter recursion.
The constructor can assign through the setter for validation.
Throw `RangeError` for out-of-range numeric values.
The getter and setter form one property on the prototype.

questions.question: Implement a static `User.fromJSON(json)` factory that parses a JSON string and returns a `User`, throwing a `SyntaxError` unchanged for bad JSON.
key_points: Static methods are called on the class, not an instance.
Use `new this(...)` so subclasses get the right type.
`JSON.parse` already throws `SyntaxError` for malformed input.
Validate the parsed shape if the input is untrusted.

questions.answer: It throws `TypeError: Cannot read properties of undefined (reading 'label')`. `handler()` is a plain call, and class methods are strict, so `this` is `undefined`. Fix with an arrow class field (`click = () => ...`), bind in the constructor (`this.click = this.click.bind(this)`), or call it as `button.click()` / pass a wrapper `() => button.click()`.
key_points: Detached methods lose their receiver.
Class methods are always strict, so `this` is `undefined`, not the global object.
Arrow class fields bind per instance.
`bind` in the constructor is the pre-fields alternative.

questions.answer: A derived constructor cannot access `this` before `super()` runs. The instance is created by the parent constructor, so `this.name = name` throws `ReferenceError: Must call super constructor ... before accessing 'this'`. The fix is to call `super(name)` first (and then optionally assign derived fields), or omit the derived constructor entirely so the default `constructor(...args) { super(...args); }` is used.
key_points: Derived constructors must call `super()` before touching `this`.
The parent constructor creates and initialises the instance.
Omitting the constructor gives a correct default that forwards args.
Only returning an object can bypass `super()`; returning a primitive still requires it.
